reason: The n-gram stream's top candidate for the verse and pure connective tissue: a relative pronoun, an auxiliary and a participle. Revelation 1:19 is John's commission to write what he has seen; 28:2 is about the worth of a book to a remnant of Israel. Nothing beyond the five function words is shared, and 'the things which' is among the commonest openings in the KJV.

sharedText: for it shall come to pass in that day
reason: A nine-word run and worth nothing, which is CONVENTIONS §9 in one line — the longest run in the chapter is its emptiest. 'It shall come to pass in that day' is the KJV's standard prophetic formula and Jeremiah 30:8 goes on to break a yoke off Israel's neck, which has no contact with churches contending over the Lord's name. The real link at 28:3 is Isaiah 44:5, which the same stream ranked below this.

sharedText: he is not a God of
reason: A genuinely tempting match and exactly inverted. Luke 20:38 is Jesus proving the resurrection from the burning bush: 'For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living.' 28:6 is a false teacher's syllogism: 'for this day he is not a God of miracles: he hath done his work.' The five shared words are identical and the argument they carry is opposite — Luke's clause is a denial made in order to affirm, and Nephi's is a denial made in order to deny. The Book of Mormon's own source for the formula is nearer to hand and is not Luke: 2 Nephi 27:23, four chapters earlier and in the Lord's own voice, reads 'I am God; and I am a God of miracles', which 28:6 contradicts word for word. Registered rather than passed over because the shared run is long, the vocabulary is content-bearing, and only reading both whole verses shows the reversal.

sharedText: to eat, and to drink, and to be merry
reason: Hardy cross-references Ecclesiastes 8:15 here alongside Isaiah 22:13, Luke 12:19 and 1 Corinthians 15:32, and for a study edition tracing the sentiment that is right. For a verbal catalogue it is superseded. Ecclesiastes 8:15 has infinitives — 'to eat, and to drink, and to be merry' — where 28:7 has Luke 12:19's imperatives, 'eat, drink, and be merry', and the KJV's only occurrence of that string is Luke's. Ecclesiastes also lacks the second half of the sentence entirely; it commends mirth as a good under the sun rather than as a consequence of tomorrow's death. The links are filed at Luke 12:19 and 1 Corinthians 15:32.

Considered and declined. 'Dig a pit for thy neighbor' looks like a proverb and there are three KJV verses that dig one — Psalm 57:6, Jeremiah 18:20 and 18:22, all in the perfect ('they have digged a pit') and all about enemies plotting against the speaker, not about a neighbour. Proverbs 26:27's 'Whoso diggeth a pit shall fall therein' is the closest in sense but shares only the verb and its object, and its point is the digger's own downfall, which 28:8 does not make. The clause is more likely a free formation on Exodus 21:33's law of the open pit than a borrowing from any of them, and no rarity count supports a link.

Hardy cross-references Isaiah 2:12-14 at this verse, and this is the shape the 2 Nephi brief warns about rather than drift: Isaiah 2 is transcribed in this same book at 2 Nephi 12, so the reader is being sent from Nephi's exposition to Nephi's own transcription of the text he is expounding. The verbal contact will not carry a link. The one distinctive phrase in Isaiah 2:12, 'proud and lofty', is a KJV singleton and does not appear at 28:12; what appears is 'lifted up', which occurs in 137 KJV verses, and 'puffed up', which is Pauline (six verses, five of them in 1 Corinthians) and not Isaiah's at all. The thematic relation is real — pride brought low is Isaiah 2's subject and 28:12-15's — and it is discharged here rather than manufactured into a figural link. A reader wanting Isaiah 2:12-14 in this book should be sent to 2 Nephi 12:12-14, where it is collated verse by verse.

The 1830's 'wo, wo, wo be unto them' is the KJV's only threefold woe in form, Revelation 8:13's 'Woe, woe, woe, to the inhabiters of the earth', and the resemblance is sharpened by 28:16 going on to speak of the Lord visiting 'the inhabitants of the earth'. It is registered rather than linked because the shared material is one interjection repeated, which is a rhetorical figure available to anyone writing a woe-oracle, and because Revelation 8:13's woes are three specific coming trumpets rather than an intensifier. The real borrowing in 28:15 is Luke 10:15's 'thrust down to hell', which is where the link sits.

'A thing of nought' occurs in Jeremiah 14:14 and in Isaiah 29:21, and the n-gram stream offered both. Isaiah wins outright: 28:16 reproduces nine consecutive words of Isaiah 29:21 — 'turn aside the just for a thing of nought' — where Jeremiah shares only the four-word phrase, embedded in a sentence about prophets who prophesy lies in the LORD's name. The chapter has also been quoting Isaiah 29 since verse 9. The link is filed at Isaiah 29:21.

The n-gram stream's only candidate for the verse and the wrong one. Job 12:5's 'him that is at ease' is the comfortable man whose thought despises the lamp of one ready to slip — a proverb about contempt, not about complacency, and Job's clause is the subject of the scorn rather than its object. 28:24 is a woe pronounced on the man at ease, and the words 'at ease in Zion' occur in exactly one KJV verse, Amos 6:1, which supplies the woe-formula as well as the ease. The link is filed there.

Hardy cross-references Isaiah 29:13 here, correctly — 'hearkeneth unto the precepts of men' is the KJV singleton 'taught by the precept of men' in Nephi's own idiom. The link is filed at 28:14, the phrase's first occurrence in this chapter, where the evidence for the mediation is: the KJV has a singular 'precept' and this book's own transcription of the verse at 2 Nephi 27:25 has the plural 'precepts', which is what 28:14, 28:26 and 28:31 all read. ADJUDICATING §4 governs the repeat — within one book a phrase is adjudicated at first use — and this entry sends the reader from Hardy's verse to ours.

reason: 'The power of God' occurs in thirteen KJV verses and the six-word run here is that phrase plus a conjunction and an article. 1 Corinthians 1:24 makes Christ the power of God to the called; 28:26 denies the power of God and the gift of the Holy Ghost together. The genuine New Testament contact in this verse is 'the gift of the Holy Ghost', confined to Acts 2:38 and 10:45, and the link is filed at the first of those.

sharedText: cursed is he that putteth his trust in man, or maketh flesh his arm
reason: Hardy cross-references Jeremiah 17:5 here and the quotation is real — 'maketh flesh his arm' occurs in exactly one KJV verse and is reproduced exactly. But it is not a fresh borrowing. 2 Nephi 4:34, in this same book and in the same narrator's voice, already reads 'cursed is he that putteth his trust in man, or maketh flesh his arm' word for word, and the link is adjudicated there with its full argument: Jeremiah's two singletons ('trusteth in man', 'maketh flesh his arm') fused with 2 Chronicles 32:8's 'arm of flesh', and Jeremiah 17:7's blessing performed in the verse before the curse is quoted. ADJUDICATING §4 governs: within one book, later occurrences are the narrator using his own formula, adjudicated at first use and registered here. What 28:31 adds is not Jeremiah's — 'or shall hearken unto the precepts of men' is Isaiah 29:13's clause again, in the plural form this chapter uses throughout, and it belongs with the link at 28:14.

sharedText: he that putteth his trust in
reason: Proverbs 28:25 and Isaiah 57:13 were the n-gram stream's two candidates, both for the six-word run 'he that putteth his trust in'. That formula is the KJV's own commonest way of saying it, and in both proposed verses the trust is placed in the LORD and the outcome is blessing — the opposite polarity to Nephi's curse. Their real relevance is that they supply the idiom into which Jeremiah 17:5's 'cursed be the man that trusteth in man' has been reworded, which is recorded in the note at 2 Nephi 4:34 where that verse is adjudicated.

Five words of prophetic boilerplate — a prepositional phrase and the KJV's commonest attribution formula. Jeremiah 31:32 concerns the broken Sinai covenant; 28:32 is a woe on the Gentiles with an offer of mercy. Covered in principle by the standing formulaic exclusions and listed only because it was the sole candidate the stream returned for the chapter's last verse, which is worth knowing when reading the Isaiah 65:2 echo filed there on manual evidence alone.
